news.title: Trump visibly deflated after reporter's stinging comeback to claim he's 'one of the greatest presidents ever'
news.text:
Donald Trump appeared taken aback when an interviewer delivered a quick-witted response to the brag that he's considered 'one of the greatest Presidents ever.'

The Commander-in-Chief spoke to Punchbowl News and was asked about how he might deal with a Democrat-controlled Congress in 2027. 

Reporter Jake Sherman asked: 'If Democrats do take over the House, it’s just going to be investigation mania. They’re going to do oversight. They could impeach you again. Do you think they will?'

'Well, a lot of people are saying I’m one of the greatest presidents ever,' Trump replied.

'They’re not saying that though,' Sherman said with a chuckle, referring to the Democrats. 

'Yeah, but they know. They see the results,' Trump responded, before rolling off a list of his accomplishments.

He cited 'more money being invested in the United States than at any time in history,' as well as construction of factories, investment in AI and companies leaving countries like Mexico, Canada, Germany, Japan and coming to the US.'

Trump, however, seems unsure whether the coalition that won him an electoral college landslide will come out for the Republican Party without him on the ballot in November.

'If I don't run, will those people go out and vote, and that's the one thing I can't tell,' Trump told Punchbowl News in an interview released Friday.

Then the President revealed his greatest open question about the coming elections and conservative voters: 'Will they vote?' 

'A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you ... they are not angry with me, but they are angry with Republicans.'

Republicans' odds of keeping control of both chambers of Congress are glum, at least according to prediction markets. 

As it stands, Republicans have less than a 20 percent chance of maintaining control of the House, per Kalshi data. In the Senate, Republicans' odds of staying in power are much more favorable at 54 percent.

But the President has a trick up his sleeve to help Republicans – he has a massive political war chest that he can deploy to help his party members campaign against their Democratic opponents.

'I could spend it on pretty much anything I want,' Trump noted in the interview, adding, 'I'm going to help Republicans.'

The President's political action committee, MAGA Inc., has $400 million in cash on hand, according to the latest Federal Election Commission filings in late June. 

The fate of Trump's remaining two years in power hinges largely on whether conservatives maintain control of Congress.

Should he lose just one chamber, either the House or the Senate, any legislation the President wants passed would need at least some Democratic support. 

The thing is, Democrats have been outspoken for years about their ardent opposition to the President and his agenda, and it is hard to see them finding common ground to push through bipartisan legislation. 

During the interview with the Congress-focused outlet, the President also spoke about his relationships with Speaker Mike Johnson and Senate Republican Leader John Thune, or lack thereof. 

Johnson, Trump said, is a 'fantastic person.' The two have worked closely together on the President's legislation in the House, and the Speaker has largely been able to deliver votes on must-pass bills for the President. 

The same cannot be said of the Senate.

When pressed on whether he would back Thune to lead the Senate Republicans again next year, the President did not offer the leader, whom he has clashed with at times, his support. 

'I don’t want to get into that,' Trump answered. 

Though Trump did note that there was no 'disconnect' between him and Thune, adding, 'I think we have a good relationship.' 

Trump has repeatedly requested that the Senate pass voter ID laws, which were already approved by the House. He sees the legislation as imperative for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections given his claims that elections have been 'rigged.' 

Thune has worked to get his Republican conference on board, but the legislation has stalled out, and the Senate Republican Leader has repeatedly told the President he does not have the votes to get it passed.
news.summary: The Commander-in-Chief spoke asked about how he might deal with a Democrat-controlled Congress in 2027.
news.author: Editor,Stephen M. Lepore

news.title: Fox News host lashes out at Americans ‘whining’ about higher gas prices in unhinged rant
news.text:
Fox News host Mark Levin lashed out Saturday night at Americans opposed to the deeply unpopular U.S. war against Iran, singling out those displeased with soaring gas and food prices.

“I remember a time when America would say, 'let's go, let's destroy that country, destroy that government!' Now it's a debate!” Levin said on his program, “Life, Liberty & Levin.”

“We don't even have a draft. Would a draft even work with young people today, I wonder! Could we even fight World War II today? We're whining about $1 of gasoline!”

Levin has been a staunch supporter of the U.S. war against Iran, and to such an extent that he broke with President Donald Trump amid the president’s attempts to secure a peace deal to end the war. He also previously invoked the fury of Trump adviser Alex Bruesewitz, who accused Levin of working on behalf of Israel to influence the U.S.-Iran peace deal.

On Saturday, however, Levin’s concentration was squarely on Americans opposed to the U.S. war against Iran, which he said did not affect the “vast majority” of Americans.

“The vast majority of us are utterly unaffected personally, our families, by what's going on in Iran with our troops,” Levin said.

The Fox News host then pivoted to mocking Americans opposed to the war: “It's going on way too long, the price of gasoline and the price of a taco now is just crazy, this has gone on long enough,” he said in a mocking tone.

Levin then compared Iran war critics unfavorably to Americans who fought in World War II.

“Affordability wasn't even an issue – victory was the issue!” he said. “Unity against an enemy was the issue. I don't think they were debating the price of a burrito or taco.”

The average U.S. household has paid nearly $450 more on energy since the conflict began on Feb. 28, according to a Moody's Analytics estimate, a hit that has cumulatively cost consumers nearly $60 billion and erased the benefit of this year's larger tax refunds. Gasoline prices climbed above $4 a gallon for the first time in more than three years, while grocery costs have climbed too, with lettuce prices up more than 16% in May and ground beef up about 12% year-over-year.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Has Brutal Clap Back To Trump Saying He's 'Full Of Sh*t'
news.text:
The Democratic nominee for U.S Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, gave a ruthless response to President Donald Trump calling him “full of shit” during an event in Las Vegas earlier this week. 

El-Sayed was asked about Trump’s remarks — including the president saying he was a gift to the Republican Party — in an interview with SkyNews’ James Matthews on Friday. The Democrat said he was a gift to the state of Michigan before delivering his brutal comeback. 

“And he (Trump) says, if you’d pardon the language, that you’re full of shit. What do you say to that?” Matthews asked.

“At least I don’t let mine go in the middle of the Oval Office,” El-Sayed said.

El-Sayed was likely making an apparent reference to jokes about the president defecating on himself. 

Trump, in addition to his expletive-laden insult of El-Sayed, leaned hard into trying to falsely paint the Democrat as a “communist.” 

“They want to go right down to the bottom of the barrel. That’s communism. They want it to be a communist country. We’re not letting them have it as a communist country. Not even for a minute,” Trump said. 

Trump and many Republicans have, as of late, been rolling out the communist moniker for Democrats ahead of the midterms.
news.author: Anthony Orrico

news.title: Trump-linked US firm prepares to drill in Greenland without permission, govt warns
news.text:
Greenland issued a "strong warning" after an American oil company connected to US President Donald Trump started preparing to sink wells in the Arctic region without any permission from local authorities. The firm's project is coming at a time when the American leader has renewed his threats to claim the vast Arctic territory.
The Greenlandic authorities began to express concern when drilling materials were brought ashore in recent days on the island's eastern coast. The move has prompted Greenland’s government to issue a “strong warning” that no approval had been granted to land the kit.
“All future logistical matters must be advised and approved by the mineral resources authority – before they are carried out,” the government said in a statement. However, two days later, Trump made a menacing post on Truth Social, showing himself looming over a Greenlandic village.
The company in question is Greenland Energy, which is based in Texas and was set up last year. They have claimed that $1 trillion of crude may lie beneath the Jameson Land region. Hence, the firm announced plans to spend $60 million drilling two wells to find out.
Greenland authorities attempt to block the drilling
However, it is pertinent to note that the Greenland authorities stopped issuing new oil licences in 2021 on environmental grounds. But despite this, a UK company called 80 Mile had secured exploration rights in Jameson Land. Greenland Energy’s corporate filings say it will take a majority stake in the project in exchange for funding the exploration, though it still needs government permission to proceed.
The American firm is retained by Phil McGraw, popularly known as Dr Phil, a prominent rightwing former chatshow host who served on Trump’s religious freedom commission, to make a documentary series that will “capture the mission of these modern-day wildcatters”.
It has also appointed the director, a US Navy veteran who is working on Golden Dome, the missile defence plan for which Trump says controlling Greenland is “vital”. Larry Swets, Greenland Energy’s chair and a big shareholder, appears to enjoy access to Trump’s circle. He has said the oil project is “not related to American annexation”.
In June, the company representatives falsely claimed to have permission for drilling at a Jameson Land community meeting. “Our enthusiasm for the project led us to communicate in a way that created confusion," Swets said at that time.
But the next month, local people in the sparsely populated region noticed a tug pulling a barge shorewards and unloading a dozen containers. “The goal was to get the equipment onshore at Nunap Qeqqa [Jameson Land] in connection with planned oil exploration drilling,” the Greenland government’s statement said. Meanwhile, the Danish investigative outlet Danwatch quoted the head of the shipping company as confirming the delivery was for Greenland Energy.
Greenland Energy in its letter to the shareholders said: "Recent high-level meetings between project leadership and Greenlandic regulatory and oversight authorities have been constructive, and we continue to be encouraged by the progress being made toward the remaining approvals required for drilling.” It said that after those discussions, just one well would be drilled to begin with.
The Greenland government's statement, on the other hand, said it “would not be proportionate” to demand the equipment be removed. An application for permission remained under processing, it added. Amidst all this, Jeff Landry, the hard-right Louisiana governor serving as Trump’s Greenland envoy, has said Greenland could be pumping oil next year.

news.title: World News | Iran's Mehr News Agency Releases Undated Video of Mojtaba Khamenei After Israeli Media Report on His Poor Health
news.text:
Tel Aviv [Israel], August 9 (ANI): Days after Israeli media claimed that Iran's Supreme Leader was in critical condition and had been rushed to a hospital, Iran's semi-official Mehr News agency released an undated video showing Mojtaba Khamenei appearing to be in good health. 

The video of Mojtaba Khamenei was published for the first time by Mehr, a semi-official news agency sponsored by the government of Iran and run by the Iranian government's Islamic Development Organisation, as an effort to negate mounting speculation over Khamenei's health and whereabouts. 

Also Read | 'Very Sad to Watch': Hunter Biden Gets Emotional While Discussing Joe Biden's Cancer Battle.

https://x.com/mehrnewsarabic/status/2086064358073696415?s=20

Earlier on Friday, Israeli media reports had claimed that Khamenei was in an "extremely critical condition". Channel 14, citing sources inside Iran, and an earlier report by The Jerusalem Post, quoting IranWire and sources close to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's administration, reported that concerns over his health were circulating within Iran's leadership.

Also Read | PM Narendra Modi Speaks With US VP JD Vance to Strengthen Bilateral Ties, Congratulates Family on New Birth.

One source cited by The Jerusalem Post had claimed, "We would not be surprised if we heard news of his martyrdom soon."

Khamenei assumed the position of Supreme Leader shortly after his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was assassinated in joint US-Israeli military strikes on February 28. Since taking office, he has not made any public appearances and has communicated exclusively through written statements.

Reports indicate he was injured and potentially disfigured in the initial strikes that targeted his father's compound, forcing him into hiding and compelling him to communicate with senior regime figures through a slow network of intermediaries to avoid targeting.

Adding to the speculation surrounding his status, President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged in a state TV interview that direct interaction with Khamenei is currently "very difficult". 

International and regional reports have repeatedly questioned his physical location and capacity. In July, Saudi news outlet al-Hadath, citing an Israeli security source, claimed that Khamenei was "not in Iran."

Around the same time, US President Donald Trump asserted in a Fox News interview that Iran's top military leadership had been eliminated, claiming that Khamenei was "90% gone" and incapacitated following the military campaign.

Iranian state officials have previously downplayed the severity of his initial injuries, but the persistent lack of live appearances or direct public addresses continues to fuel intense regional and international speculation regarding his health and leadership stability.

While Western and opposition intelligence sources have frequently suggested that he sustained severe or disfiguring injuries, leading to his total absence from live public appearances and reliance solely on written statements, Iranian state officials have offered contrasting accounts.

Representatives from Iran's Health Ministry previously characterised his initial injuries as superficial, and senior officials have maintained that he continues to provide strategic oversight and operational directives for the country. (ANI)

news.title: World News | US Pentagon Asks Defence Firms to Ramp Up Weapons Production: Report
news.text:
Washington, DC [US], August 9 (ANI): The US Defence Department has asked American defence contractors to urgently increase weapons production and speed up deliveries amid concerns over a shortage of critical munitions linked to the war with Iran, The Washington Post reported while citing a memo.

Deputy Defence Secretary Steve Feinberg told industry leaders on Wednesday they have up to 21 days to submit plans for "significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities".

Also Read | 'Very Sad to Watch': Hunter Biden Gets Emotional While Discussing Joe Biden's Cancer Battle.

"Years-long development timelines are unacceptable," Feinberg said, calling on companies to "dramatically accelerate" output and timelines.

This comes even as a Pentagon official told Al Jazeera on Saturday that US munitions stocks remain adequate.

Also Read | PM Narendra Modi Speaks With US VP JD Vance to Strengthen Bilateral Ties, Congratulates Family on New Birth.

"We have sufficient munitions for the task at hand. The department has everything it needs today to execute a war," Al Jazeera quoted Jarred Conley, principal deputy director at the Defence Department's Defence Innovation Unit, as saying. 

The interceptor shortage was said to be a key issue raised by US President Donald Trump and senior advisers before the administration decided last month to pause further escalation against Iran, Al Jazeera reported. 

Meanwhile, Trump on Thursday dismissed as "fake" a report that he confronted Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over depleted US weapons stockpiles during a meeting at Camp David, insisting he has "the utmost confidence" in his Pentagon chief.

While addressing a report published by The Washington Post, Trump stated on Truth Social that he was "extremely happy" with the performance of Hegseth and accused the news outlet of disseminating "false and completely unfounded rumours". 

"The Fake News, as usual, is spreading false and completely unfounded rumours. I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing," Trump wrote.

He lauded the execution of military operations under Hegseth, highlighting the administration's actions in Venezuela and Iran, and noted that both missions had fulfilled their objectives.

Trump further attributed rising military recruitment figures and the removal of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes to Hegseth.

Labelling The Washington Post "one of the worst media outlets in the business", Trump claimed that the publication was cautioned prior to release that its story was "completely FALSE" and characterised the coverage as "treasonous".

The Washington Post, citing sources familiar with the development, stated that Trump voiced irritation towards Hegseth during a Cabinet session at Camp David last week regarding alleged deficits in key munitions, particularly long-range missiles and air-defence interceptors, which were reportedly impacting US military strategies in the Iran conflict.

As per the report, Hegseth refuted claims of misleading the president and attributed the lack of a full briefing to Deputy Secretary of War Stephen Feinberg.

The report further asserted that the interaction highlighted Trump's mounting irritation with his Pentagon chief as the ongoing Iran conflict strained US arms reserves.

Both the White House and the Pentagon refuted the claims.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt stated that the narrative "literally never happened" and reiterated that Trump maintained "the utmost confidence" in Hegseth.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell similarly rejected the assertions, stating that Hegseth had neither misled anyone regarding US ammunition supplies nor held Feinberg responsible for potential deficits. (ANI)

news.title: US Pentagon asks defence firms to boost production of key systems amid concerns over shortage
news.text:
WASHINGTON – The Pentagon’s No. 2 official asked major US defence companies to accelerate efforts to produce and deliver key weapons systems amid new concerns about shortages and gaps exacerbated by the Iran war.

Steve Feinberg, the deputy secretary of defence, said the department is targeting accelerated or increased procurement for critical programmes including wide-area surveillance, air-defence sensors and interceptors, and missile-tracking systems.

“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” he wrote in an Aug 5 letter seen by Bloomberg to major defence companies, including Boeing, Lockheed Martin and RTX.

“We must dramatically accelerate our programme schedules and expand our production capacity now.” The Washington Post reported earlier on the letter.

There have been growing warnings about the state of US weapons stockpiles as the US military attacks Iran and repels its drone and missile strikes on American bases in the region.

US President Donald Trump has denied the US is running low on munitions, saying on Aug 6 the country has “massive amounts” of them, while warning of punishment for those who say there’s a shortage.

Even so, he also said the US has some systems “where it’s a little bit tighter, and we’re getting them in on a daily basis”, although he didn’t provide any details.

In his letter, Feinberg focused on needs beyond those related to the Iran war, including satellite communications and next-generation air-defence systems. Another priority is Lockheed Martin’s Next Generation Interceptor, a programme aimed at defending the US from intercontinental ballistic missiles.

He asked companies to submit their plans by late August “for more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production capacity” in the critical programmes he identified. BLOOMBERG

news.title: Ukraine needs at least 12 months to start making Patriots — Zelensky
news.text:
MOSCOW, August 9. /TASS/. Even if Ukraine obtains a license to produce Patriot air defense systems from the United States, launching the production will take at least one year at best, Vladimir Zelensky said.

When asked how long it would take to start the production, he said: "From 12 months to several years."

"Ukraine should obtain corresponding licenses," he told Ukrainian television. "There are certain procedures and rules in other countries, not only in the United States, but in Europe, too."

In his words, even if the license to manufacture Patriots is granted to Ukraine, it will not be able to produce interceptor missiles on its own.

During a meeting with Vladimir Zelensky on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara in June, US President Donald Trump said transfering the Patriot license to Ukraine was possible. However, in late July Trump apparently reversed his decision. The American president told reporters that the US had not agreed to letting Ukraine ·build Patriot missiles and the US must be "very careful about letting somebody build them."
news.summary: According to Vladimir Zelensky, even if the license to manufacture Patriots is granted to Ukraine, it will not be able to produce interceptor missiles on its own

news.title: The question raised inside the White House that could define America's future - opinion
news.text: Last week, I joined roughly two dozen faith leaders, writers, activists, and policy advocates inside the Eisenhower Executive Office Building for a White House Faith Office briefing.As someone who has spent years writing about antisemitism, Israel, and the role faith plays in public life, I expected discussions about religious liberty, faith-based initiatives, and public policy.Instead, I left reflecting on something much deeper: whether a constitutional republic can endure when the moral culture that sustains it begins to erode.Throughout the day, Jennifer Korn, Deputy Assistant to the President and Faith Director of the White House Faith Office, Pastor Paula White-Cain, Senior Advisor to the White House Faith Office, Border Czar Tom Homan, Dr. Sebastian Gorka, Assistant to the President and White House Staff Secretary Will Scharf, Special Assistant to the President for Jewish Outreach Martin Marks, Deputy Assistant to the President Kailee Buller, and other senior administration officials addressed the room.Their responsibilities ranged from national security and immigration to Jewish outreach, religious liberty, and combating human trafficking. Yet despite their different portfolios, they repeatedly returned to the same conviction: America's future depends not only on sound policies but on the moral and spiritual character of its people.What struck me most was not simply that God was mentioned, but how naturally He was spoken about.For nearly six and a half hours, references to God, prayer, faith, and moral responsibility arose repeatedly and without hesitation. They did not feel scripted or politically calculated. Several speakers became visibly emotional as they spoke about prayer and the role faith had played in their own lives and public service.There was no hesitation in invoking God. There was no sense that faith needed to be hidden behind carefully crafted political language. It was spoken of with sincerity, conviction, and genuine belief.Throughout the day, speaker after speaker described restoring faith to American civic life as one of the defining missions of the White House Faith Office. Whether discussing religious liberty, border security, combating human trafficking, strengthening families, or confronting antisemitism, they consistently returned to the same idea: government can protect liberty, but it cannot manufacture virtue.Whether one agrees with this administration or not, the White House Faith Office reflects a conviction that was expressed repeatedly throughout the briefing: America's deepest challenges are not merely political but moral. That is more than a policy position. It is a philosophy of government.The underlying premise is that laws can punish crime, budgets can fund programs, and executive orders can shape policy, but none of them can create character. If that premise is correct, then the long-term health of the republic ultimately depends upon the moral formation of its citizens.Listening to those presentations, I found myself thinking less about the administration and more about the Founding Fathers.US Constitution a great historical achievementThe Constitution is rightly celebrated as one of history's greatest political achievements. Yet the Framers never imagined that liberty could survive on constitutional mechanics alone. They designed a system of checks and balances because they understood the dangers of concentrated power. But they also believed that self-government required citizens capable of governing themselves.John Adams famously wrote that the Constitution was made “only for a moral and religious people” and was “wholly inadequate to the government of any other.”Whether one agrees entirely with that assessment or not, it reflects a conviction shared by many of the Founders: free institutions ultimately depend upon virtuous citizens.That observation feels remarkably relevant today.Americans spend enormous amounts of time debating inflation, immigration, education, crime, foreign policy, and the expanding role of government. Those debates matter. But perhaps they are downstream from a more fundamental question.What happens when a society no longer shares a common moral foundation?Every civilization is shaped by values. The question is never whether values will influence public life but which values will prevail. History suggests that societies rarely abandon their moral foundations all at once. One generation treats a principle as optional. The next forgets it ever existed.In my view, many progressive political and cultural movements have sought to reshape American institutions through lawful political, educational, and cultural change. Their supporters regard these efforts as expanding equality and opportunity.I see something different: a gradual replacement of the moral assumptions that undergirded the American experiment with a framework in which identity politics, expressive individualism, and an ever-expanding role for the state increasingly displace the institutions that have traditionally formed character: families, faith communities, local associations, and civic life.For American Jews, this discussion is no longer theoretical. Antisemitic assaults, harassment, intimidation, and the normalization of anti-Jewish hatred have become alarmingly common. Every act of antisemitism is the responsibility of the individual who commits it.But we should also ask what kind of civic culture allows hatred to become normalized and what moral vocabulary remains available to condemn it consistently, regardless of who the victim happens to be.Alexis de Tocqueville warned that democracies rarely lose their freedoms through dramatic revolutions. More often, they drift toward greater centralization as citizens gradually transfer responsibilities once carried by families, religious communities, and local institutions to the state.Friedrich Hayek similarly cautioned that liberty is often surrendered incrementally, each expansion of authority justified by the crisis of the moment until the destination becomes visible only in hindsight. Their warnings were not about one political party or one election. They were about human nature.One need not agree with every policy advanced by President Donald Trump to recognize the significance of the question his administration is asking. The White House Faith Office reflects a belief expressed repeatedly throughout the briefing: that political freedom cannot endure indefinitely if the moral culture that sustains self-government continues to erode.The Constitution is not weakened only when it is openly violated. It can also be hollowed out gradually when each generation accepts just enough civic and moral decline that the next mistakes the exception for the norm.As I left the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, I realized that the most important conversation I had heard that day was not about a single policy initiative. It was about whether America still believes that virtue, faith, and moral responsibility are indispensable to the survival of a constitutional republic.America's future will not be determined solely by the laws we pass or the elections we win. It will also be determined by the moral convictions we preserve, the truths we are willing to defend, and the values we pass on to our children.That was the deeper lesson I took away from my day inside the White House Faith Office. The speakers came from different backgrounds and carried different responsibilities, yet they shared a common conviction: that no constitutional republic can long endure if it loses the moral foundation upon which its freedoms rest. Whether Americans ultimately embrace or reject that premise may prove to be one of the defining questions of our time.Because in the end, a Constitution can preserve a nation's freedom. Only its people can preserve the moral character that allows that freedom to endure.The writer is an author and strategist whose work explores Jewish life, culture, and public affairs. She is the founder of 250Shabbat, a grassroots initiative strengthening Jewish identity through the shared experience of Shabbat, and host of The Silent Revolution podcast.
news.author: Linda Argalgi Sadacka

news.title: Pentagon in Weapons Race Against Time as US Munitions Stocks Plunge Amid Iran War
news.text: The Pentagon has urged defence companies to rapidly increase the production and delivery of weapons, including munitions in short supply following the war with Iran. Deputy Defence Secretary Steve Feinberg gave US defence companies 21 days to submit plans to "drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities", according to a Defense Department memo cited by The Washington Post. "Years-long development cycles are not acceptable," Feinberg wrote. "We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now." The memo is the latest move by the Pentagon and White House to address concerns over depleted US weapons stocks. The weapons shortage has become a source of tension between President Donald Trump and the Defense Department, according to people familiar with the issue cited by The Washington Post. Trump said on Thursday that the US had "massive amounts" of munitions. "Large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed," he wrote on Truth Social. But defence experts have warned that rebuilding US stocks could take time and may depend on Congress approving additional defence spending. During the first month of the war with Iran, the US fired more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and more than 1,000 Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors, according to The Washington Post. The US also used more than 1,300 Army tactical ballistic missiles during the initial weeks of fighting. An analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that the global inventory of Patriot missiles had fallen from about 2,200 before the war to fewer than 827 as of last week. The number of THAAD missiles had fallen from 452 to fewer than 278, according to the analysis. Pentagon Seeks Faster Production The Pentagon has already taken steps to increase weapons production. On Monday, the department announced a framework agreement with Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin to increase production of Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) and THAAD missiles. Last week, Lockheed Martin received a contract worth up to $58.6bn to triple production of PAC-3 missiles by 2030. The Pentagon also announced framework agreements in May with defence technology companies including Anduril, Castelion, CoAspire, Leidos and Zone 5 to "aggressively expand" US military strike capabilities and purchase low-cost missiles. In late June, the department hosted leaders from several Silicon Valley start-ups as it sought to increase the role of newer companies in rebuilding US weapons supplies. The agreements are legal but non-binding arrangements that signal the Pentagon's intention to buy weapons. They still require congressional funding before becoming final contracts. "They are agreements to agree, and so they’re not contracts," Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told The Washington Post. "Almost nothing has been contracted, and that’s the problem." Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said working with defence companies to accelerate production was not a new policy. "Working directly with industry leaders to accelerate production is not new. It has been the clear intent of the President and this Secretary from the start," he said. He confirmed that the Feinberg memo "is real" and said it "will inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding". He added that the directive was "entirely consistent with our ongoing push to rebuild the defense industrial base". Trump Seeks More Funding The White House has also sought to encourage the defence industry to push for increased military spending. In late July, major defence contractors and Silicon Valley weapons companies were invited to the White House for a meeting with senior administration officials, including Mr Trump's chief of staff Susie Wiles, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and White House Legislative Affairs Director James Braid. Companies including Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Boeing, Anduril and Palantir were represented at the meeting, according to people familiar with the event. Executives were asked to directly lobby lawmakers to increase defence spending through congressional reconciliation, the sources said. The Pentagon's push comes as Hegseth seeks to overhaul the US military's acquisition system and make it more responsive to wartime demands. Speaking at the National War College in Washington in November, Hegseth said US industry needed to be given greater freedom to develop weapons and technology. "American industry and its innovative spirit are begging to be unleashed to solve our most complex and dangerous warfighting problems," he said. "We need to get out of our own way, out of your way and enter into real partnership with you rather than overprescribe and decelerate your natural progress."
news.summary: There have been concerns over depleted US weapon stocks and the tensions between President Trump and the Defense Department regarding military supplies
news.author: Rounak Bagchi

news.title: Iran's Mehr News agency releases undated video of Mojtaba Khamenei after Israeli Media report on his poor health
news.text:
Tel Aviv [Israel], August 9 (ANI): Days after Israeli media claimed that Iran's Supreme Leader was in critical condition and had been rushed to a hospital, Iran's semi-official Mehr News agency released an undated video showing Mojtaba Khamenei appearing to be in good health. The video of Mojtaba Khamenei was published for the first time by Mehr, a semi-official news agency sponsored by the government of Iran and run by the Iranian government's Islamic Development Organisation, as an effort to negate mounting speculation over Khamenei's health and whereabouts.

— وكالة مهر للأنباء (@mehrnewsarabic) August 8, 2026

Earlier on Friday, Israeli media reports had claimed that Khamenei was in an "extremely critical condition". Channel 14, citing sources inside Iran, and an earlier report by The Jerusalem Post, quoting IranWire and sources close to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's administration, reported that concerns over his health were circulating within Iran's leadership.One source cited by The Jerusalem Post had claimed, "We would not be surprised if we heard news of his martyrdom soon."Khamenei assumed the position of Supreme Leader shortly after his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was assassinated in joint US-Israeli military strikes on February 28. Since taking office, he has not made any public appearances and has communicated exclusively through written statements.Reports indicate he was injured and potentially disfigured in the initial strikes that targeted his father's compound, forcing him into hiding and compelling him to communicate with senior regime figures through a slow network of intermediaries to avoid targeting.Adding to the speculation surrounding his status, President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged in a state TV interview that direct interaction with Khamenei is currently "very difficult". International and regional reports have repeatedly questioned his physical location and capacity. In July, Saudi news outlet al-Hadath, citing an Israeli security source, claimed that Khamenei was "not in Iran."Around the same time, US President Donald Trump asserted in a Fox News interview that Iran's top military leadership had been eliminated, claiming that Khamenei was "90% gone" and incapacitated following the military campaign.Iranian state officials have previously downplayed the severity of his initial injuries, but the persistent lack of live appearances or direct public addresses continues to fuel intense regional and international speculation regarding his health and leadership stability.While Western and opposition intelligence sources have frequently suggested that he sustained severe or disfiguring injuries, leading to his total absence from live public appearances and reliance solely on written statements, Iranian state officials have offered contrasting accounts.Representatives from Iran's Health Ministry previously characterised his initial injuries as superficial, and senior officials have maintained that he continues to provide strategic oversight and operational directives for the country. (ANI)

news.title: Accused MAGA lawmaker defies Trump allies in move that could aid Dems: report
news.text:
Rep. Max Miller (R-OH), who in recent days has faced mounting pressure to drop his re-election campaign amid accusations of abuse, confirmed to The New York Times Saturday that he would stay in the race, a move that GOP leadership fears could hand Democrats an easy midterm victory.

Miller has been accused of physically abusing his ex-wife and 2-year-old daughter, allegations he’s vehemently denied. He was pressed by President Donald Trump to “look carefully at his odds” of winning, the Times reported, which he noted were not “looking good.”

The deadline for Miller to resign is Saturday evening at the latest to give “local party chairs enough time to name a replacement on the ballot by Monday at 4 p.m.,” the Times reported. With Miller’s confirmation that he intends to stay in the race – a decision at odds with Trump allies who’ve pressed the president to call on Miller to drop out – the Ohio Republican may very well help Democrats turn the district blue.

“Top Republicans worry [Miller and Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC), who was accused of inappropriate conduct toward young female staffers] could cost the party a key pair of seats in November,” Punchbowl News previously reported.

Miller is now poised to face Democratic congressional candidate Brian Poindexter, who as of Thursday was leading Miller by 14 points.

“The Ohio Republican Party and local party chairs stayed publicly quiet this week, for the most part, declining to answer questions about whether they supported Mr. Miller’s candidacy,” the Times’ report reads.

“If Mr. Miller had withdrawn, they would have had to call a meeting by the end of Saturday to replace him, under state law. Matt Miller, the chairman of Ashland County and the mayor of Ashland, who is not related to the congressman, said on Saturday that no such meeting had been scheduled.”

news.title: World News | PM Modi Speaks to JD Vance, Discusses Ways to Deepen India-US Partnership
news.text:
New Delhi [India], August 9 (ANI): Prime Minister Narendra Modi received a phone call from US Vice President JD Vance, during which both leaders discussed ways to deepen the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership across key areas.

On Saturday, in a post on X, PM Modi wrote, "Received a phone call from US Vice President JD Vance. We discussed ways to further deepen India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership across key areas."

The Prime Minister also extended his congratulations to the US Vice President and the Second Lady on the birth of their son. 

Also Read | PM Narendra Modi Speaks With US VP JD Vance to Strengthen Bilateral Ties, Congratulates Family on New Birth.

"Warmly congratulated him and the Second Lady on the birth of their son and conveyed best wishes to the entire family," the post added.

This comes after Vance on Saturday (local time) said that Washington is working to establish a route allowing commercial ships to safely pass through the Strait of Hormuz, while continuing to pressure Iran amid ongoing tensions in the region. 

Speaking to Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany on 'Saturday in America', Vance said the plan includes Iran's commitment not to fire on commercial ships, he says, adding that Tehran informed Washington it would allow the maximum flow of oil through the strait but "we don't trust it".

"We're talking to the Iranians, of course. We're trying to maximise the amount of oil and gas that is coming out of the Strait of Hormuz," Vance said. 

Meanwhile, the US Senate passed a bipartisan bill on Friday that could authorise Donald Trump to levy tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries, including India and China, that continue importing Russian oil and gas, maintaining that such trade helps sustain Moscow's economy and fund its military operations in Ukraine.

The Senate approved the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by an overwhelming 86-11 vote. Named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, one of its principal architects, the legislation aims to escalate economic pressure on Russia and Iran while targeting nations that maintain major energy trade ties with Moscow.

Under the provisions, the US president would be granted discretionary authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the world's top five buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas.

Beyond targeting foreign energy buyers, the legislation outlines fresh sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior political and military officials, financial institutions, energy developments and connected entities linked to Russia's war effort.

It further extends US sanctions to older and reflagged oil tankers allegedly utilised by Russia to circumvent global restrictions and maintain energy export revenues. The broader objective is to restrict the financial flows supporting Russia's economy and military campaign.

The legislation empowers the US president to enforce tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported from the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas. India remains one of the largest buyers of Russian crude globally, alongside China.

The measure seeks to present energy-importing nations with a choice between continuing to purchase discounted Russian energy or retaining access to the lucrative US market.

India expanded its procurement of discounted Russian crude following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022 to secure national energy requirements during global market turmoil.

While Russia was historically not a traditional primary supplier for India, the availability of discounted crude allowed Indian refiners to optimise raw material costs and ensure uninterrupted domestic supplies, particularly amid transit disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

New Delhi has consistently maintained that its energy procurement strategy is guided strictly by national interest, energy security and the imperative to guarantee affordable and reliable energy for its citizens. (ANI)

news.title: Will Asia turn its back on Fifa chief Gianni Infantino amid global divide in football?
news.text:
As the fight for the heart and soul of world football rumbles into a second weekend, a much clearer picture of the battle lines has started to emerge and in some cases divisions within camps are already obvious.
Firmly in the anti-Gianni Infantino brigade stands Uefa, and, as of Friday, on the other side of the field the football authorities of Africa and South America.
In a statement that came as little surprise, Norway’s federation said the trust was gone and asked the Fifa president to resign. The head of the country’s governing body, Lise Klaveness, is among those many would back to take the under-fire Infantino’s place.
The European governing body, meanwhile, said it was not satisfied with the apology that came this week, and maintained that the threat to boycott Fifa events still stood.
But the Swiss lawyer has friends around the world, and those in the South American Football Confederation (Conmebol) have nailed their colours firmly to the 56-year-old’s mast.
A guest at Friday’s inauguration of Colombia’s hard-right president Abelardo de la Espriella in Cali, a smiling Infantino was pictured alongside Conmebol president Alejandro Dominguez and the head of the Colombian federation, Ramon Jesurun.

Support has also come from Argentina, Paraguay, Venezuela and Ecuador, while Mexico, one of the co-hosts of this summer’s World Cup, said it “supports president Infantino’s leadership”.
And then there are those, outwardly at least, who are still playing the waiting game, such as the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), and their Concacaf counterparts in North America.
The former is not a house united by any means. While the Jordan FA has been vocal in its opposition, going so far as to accuse Fifa of blackmail and bullying, Indonesia and the Philippines have come out in support of the game’s top administrator.
For many across the poorer regions, the millions of dollars offered as part of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) are too much to ignore, and the Philippine Football Federation said it “continues to support the goal behind it, championed by Fifa President Gianni Infantino: expanding commercial and financial assistance to all 211 member associations, especially smaller markets like the Philippines”.
Aside from an initial statement against the plan, the AFC has remained publicly silent, committing to neither side. Behind closed doors, however, a different picture emerges.
According to a source with intimate knowledge of the inner workings of the confederation, should a challenger from Asia stand, they would likely secure the governing body’s backing.
While AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who lost narrowly to Infantino in 2016, would have support, the source said Nasser Al-Khelaifi was the popular choice.
However, people close to Al-Khelaifi have said he “has no ambition” to be Fifa boss, and his role as chairman of Qatar Sports Investments makes a bid unlikely, given the Middle East country said it fully supported Infantino’s “unwavering efforts to advance football around the globe”.
And despite the continuing unease over some of his behaviour, and Iran’s treatment at the World Cup, Infantino could yet keep Asia’s vote, with the president preferred to Prince Ali bin Al-Hussein of Jordan, who the source said was “notoriously difficult” to deal with.
The heads of many smaller member associations in the region, such as Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Yemen and Bhutan, had a secret meeting with Infantino in New York around the time of the World Cup final.
People present at the meeting, which was also attended by US President Donald Trump, say the associations were promised US$8 million each before the next election, although there was no mention of the FFE at the time.
Fifa had said it could raise as much as US$4.2 billion based on a valuation of US$20 billion for a new commercial venture, with the money coming from private equity. There were claims as much as US$20 million could flow into each association’s bank account almost immediately, with more to follow between now and 2030.

“A number of the Asian associations do not object to FFE,” a source said. “They don’t have the financial clout of their big European equivalents and some in South America, and want the money.”
It was at the meeting in New York that Trump reportedly suggested Infantino could be the next secretary general of the United Nations, and in many ways, with one member association, one vote, Fifa looks like it is again experiencing what Herve Verhoosel called “a multilateral political negotiation with a football attached to it”.
Verhoosel, who is based in Thailand, spent more than 20 years working with the UN in various senior communication roles and said the situation reminded him of a “difficult UN Security Council negotiation”.
“Statements and counterstatements. Public support and private reservations. Confederations and individual associations taking positions. Alliances. Personal relationships. Competing interests. Pressure. Last-minute discussions. People trying to establish who supports whom and, ultimately, counting votes,” Verhoosel added.
Infantino has also built up credit in Asia, especially with Erick Thohir, chairman of the Football Association of Indonesia, who joined the Philippines in backing the FFE plan.
Pointing to the world governing body’s reaction after the Kanjuruhan Stadium disaster in 2002, when 135 people were killed, and the avoidance of sanctions when Indonesia refused to host Israel for the men’s Under-20 World Cup, Thohir said football in the country had “achieved so many successes thanks to the community, government, and Fifa working together. We should be grateful, especially to Fifa”.
The immediate draw of millions of dollars in financing aside, Verhoosel suggested there could be an opportunity for Asia in the divisions in the game.
“They can use the fact that their votes matter to demand more,” he said. “But short-term interests can become confused with long-term interests.
“Perhaps that is the opportunity hidden inside this crisis. Not US$20 billion versus no US$20 billion. Not Fifa versus Uefa. Not personalities against personalities.
“But 211 associations asking what kind of Fifa they want to leave behind.”

However, people close to Al-Khelaifi have said he “has no ambition” to be Fifa boss, and his role as chairman of Qatar Sports Investments makes a bid unlikely, given the Middle East country said it fully supported Infantino’s “unwavering efforts to advance football around the globe”.
And despite the continuing unease over some of his behaviour, and Iran’s treatment at the World Cup, Infantino could yet keep Asia’s vote, with the president preferred to Prince Ali bin Al-Hussein of Jordan, who the source said was “notoriously difficult” to deal with.
The heads of many smaller member associations in the region, such as Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Yemen and Bhutan, had a secret meeting with Infantino in New York around the time of the World Cup final.
People present at the meeting, which was also attended by US President Donald Trump, say the associations were promised US$8 million each before the next election, although there was no mention of the FFE at the time.
Fifa had said it could raise as much as US$4.2 billion based on a valuation of US$20 billion for a new commercial venture, with the money coming from private equity. There were claims as much as US$20 million could flow into each association’s bank account almost immediately, with more to follow between now and 2030.

“A number of the Asian associations do not object to FFE,” a source said. “They don’t have the financial clout of their big European equivalents and some in South America, and want the money.”
It was at the meeting in New York that Trump reportedly suggested Infantino could be the next secretary general of the United Nations, and in many ways, with one member association, one vote, Fifa looks like it is again experiencing what Herve Verhoosel called “a multilateral political negotiation with a football attached to it”.
Verhoosel, who is based in Thailand, spent more than 20 years working with the UN in various senior communication roles and said the situation reminded him of a “difficult UN Security Council negotiation”.
“Statements and counterstatements. Public support and private reservations. Confederations and individual associations taking positions. Alliances. Personal relationships. Competing interests. Pressure. Last-minute discussions. People trying to establish who supports whom and, ultimately, counting votes,” Verhoosel added.
Infantino has also built up credit in Asia, especially with Erick Thohir, chairman of the Football Association of Indonesia, who joined the Philippines in backing the FFE plan.
Pointing to the world governing body’s reaction after the Kanjuruhan Stadium disaster in 2002, when 135 people were killed, and the avoidance of sanctions when Indonesia refused to host Israel for the men’s Under-20 World Cup, Thohir said football in the country had “achieved so many successes thanks to the community, government, and Fifa working together. We should be grateful, especially to Fifa”.
The immediate draw of millions of dollars in financing aside, Verhoosel suggested there could be an opportunity for Asia in the divisions in the game.
“They can use the fact that their votes matter to demand more,” he said. “But short-term interests can become confused with long-term interests.
“Perhaps that is the opportunity hidden inside this crisis. Not US$20 billion versus no US$20 billion. Not Fifa versus Uefa. Not personalities against personalities.
“But 211 associations asking what kind of Fifa they want to leave behind.”

 "Zero experience, running govt like headless chickens": AIADMK's Kovai Sathyan slams Tamil Nadu govt amid Cauvery row

 Chennai (Tamil Nadu) [India], August 9 (ANI): All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) national spokesperson Kovai Sathyan on Saturday criticised the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) leadership over its focus on the delimitation issue, alleging that the state's water crisis and the concerns of farmers should be given priority.
 Speaking to ANI, Sathyan said that several districts in Tamil Nadu are dependent on the Cauvery River and farmers are facing a shortage of water.
 He accused the TVK leadership of lacking governance experience and said that the government was not focusing on the state's pressing issues.
 'It's a curse for Tamil Nadu, because people (TVK leaders) with zero experience in governance are running the government like headless chickens. The priority now is water. Farmers are starving without water, and there are 12 districts that are dependent on the Cauvery River. Rather than addressing that issue, Joseph Vijay is taking up the issue of delimitation,' Sathyan said. 
 'It clearly indicates the misplaced priorities of this government. There is no difference between this government and the DMK. They only believe in reels, advertisements, and renaming and rebranding the successful schemes of AIADMK,' he added.
 On the delimitation exercise, Sathyan said AIADMK's position was that Tamil Nadu's proportionate representation in Parliament should not decline from the existing level, irrespective of any increase in the total number of seats.
 He said Tamil Nadu currently accounts for 7.16 per cent of the total representation in Parliament and asserted that the proportion should remain unchanged after delimitation. He also referred to Union Home Minister Amit Shah's assurance on the matter.
 'As far as this delimitation is concerned, it's pretty much clear that 59 seats will be the number for Tamil Nadu with respect to the 850 MPs that will turn out to be X per cent. Our demand is very clear with respect to this delimitation. The proportionate representation of Tamil Nadu stands at 7.16% with the present number of MPs. Whatever number it may increase, it should not change. And our Home Minister, Amit Shah, has assured that it will not change.'
 Sathyan also criticised TVK chief Vijay for directly reaching out to AIADMK MPs over the delimitation issue instead of approaching the party leadership.
 He said the move reflected what he termed a lack of organisational maturity within TVK.
 'Since our stand is pretty clear, I really don't understand who has advised Joseph Vijay to call up our MPs directly and invite them rather than addressing it to the party leader, rather than respecting the organisational hierarchy. It clearly shows how immature and incompetent TVK is,' Sathyan said. (ANI)

 Browns' revamped offensive line room learning to play together

 The group has used the offseason programs and training camp to build chemistry
 Brian D'Aguanno
 The Browns overhauled their offensive line this offseason, signing TTytus Howard, C/GElgton Jenkinsand GZion Johnsonin free agency. They also drafted TSpencer Fanowith the ninth overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. With the additions, the offensive line will feature key new pieces this season.
 Through the offseason program and 10 days of training camp, head coach Todd Monken and his coaching staff have utilized this time to evaluate different offensive line combinations as they work towards solidifying a starting five.
 "It starts with the puretalent,they'vegot to be able to get the job done and then you fit it together," Monken said. "You'rejust working through it, trying to find the best five. Then once you get there,you'vegot to make it all fit together."
 The Browns' new room is quickly learning to play alongside one another. The group is focused on putting in the work every day to be successful this season, even as they have worked through different combinations to combat injuries and evaluate players at different positions.
 For Johnson, though, change on the offensive line is nothing new. Going into Week 18 last season, the Chargers played with 29 different offensive line combinations, the third most in the NFL. He has experience building chemistry with an offensive line that has had limited time together.
 "Turnover and having different guys coming in, that's a natural thing for me," Johnson said. "But at the end of the day, we just need to establish that culture in our room and I think we're working at that every single day. And whether it's a guy that's played a lot of football like Tytus or Elgton or a guy who's a rookie like Spencer, everybody's just attacking and working on getting better every single day."
 The Browns have rotated Fano and TDawand Jonesat left tackle with the first team during training camp. KT Leveston has taken snaps at right guard while G Tevin Jenkins missed practice time. CLuke Wyplerhas also worked with the first team while CParker Brailsfordand Jenkins have missed time in training camp. Rotating in different players at those positions has helped with the new personnel adjustment curve, according to Howard.
 "It's definitely important to build that camaraderie together, that consistency of playing together," Howard said. "I think that's why I feel like it's been a great opportunity this camp to see a lot of guys rotate in. So, a lot of guys may be able to play against, play with guys, play beside different guys, and you get a chance to see how that player is and how you fit together. So, us being able to get the reps in camp, is only going to help us out when the season comes."
 As training camp has progressed, the offensive line has limited the Browns' dominant defensive line more. During a live pass rush drill at the end of practice on Aug. 6, the offensive line kept the pocket clean multiple times. Fano also won two out of three reps against DEJared Verse.
 The run game has also started to open up in recent practices as the Browns moved through different installations. RBQuinshon Judkinsstacked multiple impressive runs, courtesy of lanes created by the offensive line, during practice on Aug. 5 and Aug. 6.
 "I think we're improving every day," Howard said. "It's a good (defensive) line, so obviously sometimes it's going to be back and forth, but I feel like as the offensive line we're growing every day, getting better as a unit, as both run and pass, and that's the goal to get better every day. So, when game one comes, we're ready to block all game."
 The improvement starts with the mentality of the unit, instilled by offensive line coach George Warhop. He demands the best out of each offensive lineman, eliminating complacency. It doesn't matter if the player is a veteran like Howard or a rookie like Fano, Warhop expects the same.
 With a new offensive line group quickly learning to play together, the entire room is establishing what they want their identity to be this season.
 "We just need to figure outwho'sgoing to be our starting five, and we need to play like we want to play; play like the Browns," Warhop said. "Be physical, be tough and make guys deal with us."

 US Pentagon asks defence firms to ramp up weapons production: Report

 Washington, DC [US], August 9 (ANI): The US Defence Department has asked American defence contractors to urgently increase weapons production and speed up deliveries amid concerns over a shortage of critical munitions linked to the war with Iran, The Washington Post reported while citing a memo.
 Deputy Defence Secretary Steve Feinberg told industry leaders on Wednesday they have up to 21 days to submit plans for 'significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities'.
 'Years-long development timelines are unacceptable,' Feinberg said, calling on companies to 'dramatically accelerate' output and timelines.
 This comes even as a Pentagon official told Al Jazeera on Saturday that US munitions stocks remain adequate.
 'We have sufficient munitions for the task at hand. The department has everything it needs today to execute a war,' Al Jazeera quoted Jarred Conley, principal deputy director at the Defence Department's Defence Innovation Unit, as saying. 
 The interceptor shortage was said to be a key issue raised by US President Donald Trump and senior advisers before the administration decided last month to pause further escalation against Iran, Al Jazeera reported. 
 Meanwhile, Trump on Thursday dismissed as 'fake' a report that he confronted Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over depleted US weapons stockpiles during a meeting at Camp David, insisting he has 'the utmost confidence' in his Pentagon chief.
 While addressing a report published by The Washington Post, Trump stated on Truth Social that he was 'extremely happy' with the performance of Hegseth and accused the news outlet of disseminating 'false and completely unfounded rumours'. 
 'The Fake News, as usual, is spreading false and completely unfounded rumours. I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,' Trump wrote.
 He lauded the execution of military operations under Hegseth, highlighting the administration's actions in Venezuela and Iran, and noted that both missions had fulfilled their objectives.
 Trump further attributed rising military recruitment figures and the removal of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes to Hegseth.
 Labelling The Washington Post 'one of the worst media outlets in the business', Trump claimed that the publication was cautioned prior to release that its story was 'completely FALSE' and characterised the coverage as 'treasonous'.
 The Washington Post, citing sources familiar with the development, stated that Trump voiced irritation towards Hegseth during a Cabinet session at Camp David last week regarding alleged deficits in key munitions, particularly long-range missiles and air-defence interceptors, which were reportedly impacting US military strategies in the Iran conflict.
 As per the report, Hegseth refuted claims of misleading the president and attributed the lack of a full briefing to Deputy Secretary of War Stephen Feinberg.
 The report further asserted that the interaction highlighted Trump's mounting irritation with his Pentagon chief as the ongoing Iran conflict strained US arms reserves.
 Both the White House and the Pentagon refuted the claims.
 White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt stated that the narrative 'literally never happened' and reiterated that Trump maintained 'the utmost confidence' in Hegseth.
 Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell similarly rejected the assertions, stating that Hegseth had neither misled anyone regarding US ammunition supplies nor held Feinberg responsible for potential deficits. (ANI)

 Iran's Mehr News agency releases undated video of Mojtaba Khamenei after Israeli Media report on his poor health

 Tel Aviv [Israel], August 9 (ANI): Days after Israeli media claimed that Iran's Supreme Leader was in critical condition and had been rushed to a hospital, Iran's semi-official Mehr News agency released an undated video showing Mojtaba Khamenei appearing to be in good health. 
 The video of Mojtaba Khamenei was published for the first time by Mehr, a semi-official news agency sponsored by the government of Iran and run by the Iranian government's Islamic Development Organisation, as an effort to negate mounting speculation over Khamenei's health and whereabouts. 

 Earlier on Friday, Israeli media reports had claimed that Khamenei was in an 'extremely critical condition'. Channel 14, citing sources inside Iran, and an earlier report by The Jerusalem Post, quoting IranWire and sources close to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's administration, reported that concerns over his health were circulating within Iran's leadership.
 One source cited by The Jerusalem Post had claimed, 'We would not be surprised if we heard news of his martyrdom soon.'
 Khamenei assumed the position of Supreme Leader shortly after his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was assassinated in joint US-Israeli military strikes on February 28. Since taking office, he has not made any public appearances and has communicated exclusively through written statements.
 Reports indicate he was injured and potentially disfigured in the initial strikes that targeted his father's compound, forcing him into hiding and compelling him to communicate with senior regime figures through a slow network of intermediaries to avoid targeting.
 Adding to the speculation surrounding his status, President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged in a state TV interview that direct interaction with Khamenei is currently 'very difficult'. 
 International and regional reports have repeatedly questioned his physical location and capacity. In July, Saudi news outlet al-Hadath, citing an Israeli security source, claimed that Khamenei was 'not in Iran.'
 Around the same time, US President Donald Trump asserted in a Fox News interview that Iran's top military leadership had been eliminated, claiming that Khamenei was '90% gone' and incapacitated following the military campaign.
 Iranian state officials have previously downplayed the severity of his initial injuries, but the persistent lack of live appearances or direct public addresses continues to fuel intense regional and international speculation regarding his health and leadership stability.
 While Western and opposition intelligence sources have frequently suggested that he sustained severe or disfiguring injuries, leading to his total absence from live public appearances and reliance solely on written statements, Iranian state officials have offered contrasting accounts.
 Representatives from Iran's Health Ministry previously characterised his initial injuries as superficial, and senior officials have maintained that he continues to provide strategic oversight and operational directives for the country. (ANI)

news.title: US Pentagon asks defence firms to ramp up weapons production: Report
news.text:
Washington, DC [US], August 9 (ANI): The US Defence Department has asked American defence contractors to urgently increase weapons production and speed up deliveries amid concerns over a shortage of critical munitions linked to the war with Iran, The Washington Post reported while citing a memo.

Deputy Defence Secretary Steve Feinberg told industry leaders on Wednesday they have up to 21 days to submit plans for 'significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities'.

'Years-long development timelines are unacceptable,' Feinberg said, calling on companies to 'dramatically accelerate' output and timelines.

This comes even as a Pentagon official told Al Jazeera on Saturday that US munitions stocks remain adequate.

'We have sufficient munitions for the task at hand. The department has everything it needs today to execute a war,' Al Jazeera quoted Jarred Conley, principal deputy director at the Defence Department's Defence Innovation Unit, as saying. 

The interceptor shortage was said to be a key issue raised by US President Donald Trump and senior advisers before the administration decided last month to pause further escalation against Iran, Al Jazeera reported. 

Meanwhile, Trump on Thursday dismissed as 'fake' a report that he confronted Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over depleted US weapons stockpiles during a meeting at Camp David, insisting he has 'the utmost confidence' in his Pentagon chief.

While addressing a report published by The Washington Post, Trump stated on Truth Social that he was 'extremely happy' with the performance of Hegseth and accused the news outlet of disseminating 'false and completely unfounded rumours'. 

'The Fake News, as usual, is spreading false and completely unfounded rumours. I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,' Trump wrote.

He lauded the execution of military operations under Hegseth, highlighting the administration's actions in Venezuela and Iran, and noted that both missions had fulfilled their objectives.

Trump further attributed rising military recruitment figures and the removal of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes to Hegseth.

Labelling The Washington Post 'one of the worst media outlets in the business', Trump claimed that the publication was cautioned prior to release that its story was 'completely FALSE' and characterised the coverage as 'treasonous'.

The Washington Post, citing sources familiar with the development, stated that Trump voiced irritation towards Hegseth during a Cabinet session at Camp David last week regarding alleged deficits in key munitions, particularly long-range missiles and air-defence interceptors, which were reportedly impacting US military strategies in the Iran conflict.

As per the report, Hegseth refuted claims of misleading the president and attributed the lack of a full briefing to Deputy Secretary of War Stephen Feinberg.

The report further asserted that the interaction highlighted Trump's mounting irritation with his Pentagon chief as the ongoing Iran conflict strained US arms reserves.

Both the White House and the Pentagon refuted the claims.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt stated that the narrative 'literally never happened' and reiterated that Trump maintained 'the utmost confidence' in Hegseth.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell similarly rejected the assertions, stating that Hegseth had neither misled anyone regarding US ammunition supplies nor held Feinberg responsible for potential deficits. (ANI)

Washington, DC [US], August 9 (ANI): The US Defence Department has asked American defence contractors to urgently increase weapons production and speed up deliveries amid concerns over a shortage of critical munitions linked to the war with Iran, The Washington Post reported while citing a memo.Deputy Defence Secretary Steve Feinberg told industry leaders on Wednesday they have up to 21 days to submit plans for "significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities"."Years-long development timelines are unacceptable," Feinberg said, calling on companies to "dramatically accelerate" output and timelines.This comes even as a Pentagon official told Al Jazeera on Saturday that US munitions stocks remain adequate."We have sufficient munitions for the task at hand. The department has everything it needs today to execute a war," Al Jazeera quoted Jarred Conley, principal deputy director at the Defence Department's Defence Innovation Unit, as saying. The interceptor shortage was said to be a key issue raised by US President Donald Trump and senior advisers before the administration decided last month to pause further escalation against Iran, Al Jazeera reported. Meanwhile, Trump on Thursday dismissed as "fake" a report that he confronted Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over depleted US weapons stockpiles during a meeting at Camp David, insisting he has "the utmost confidence" in his Pentagon chief.While addressing a report published by The Washington Post, Trump stated on Truth Social that he was "extremely happy" with the performance of Hegseth and accused the news outlet of disseminating "false and completely unfounded rumours". "The Fake News, as usual, is spreading false and completely unfounded rumours. I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing," Trump wrote.

He lauded the execution of military operations under Hegseth, highlighting the administration's actions in Venezuela and Iran, and noted that both missions had fulfilled their objectives.Trump further attributed rising military recruitment figures and the removal of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes to Hegseth.Labelling The Washington Post "one of the worst media outlets in the business", Trump claimed that the publication was cautioned prior to release that its story was "completely FALSE" and characterised the coverage as "treasonous".The Washington Post, citing sources familiar with the development, stated that Trump voiced irritation towards Hegseth during a Cabinet session at Camp David last week regarding alleged deficits in key munitions, particularly long-range missiles and air-defence interceptors, which were reportedly impacting US military strategies in the Iran conflict.As per the report, Hegseth refuted claims of misleading the president and attributed the lack of a full briefing to Deputy Secretary of War Stephen Feinberg.The report further asserted that the interaction highlighted Trump's mounting irritation with his Pentagon chief as the ongoing Iran conflict strained US arms reserves.Both the White House and the Pentagon refuted the claims.White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt stated that the narrative "literally never happened" and reiterated that Trump maintained "the utmost confidence" in Hegseth.Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell similarly rejected the assertions, stating that Hegseth had neither misled anyone regarding US ammunition supplies nor held Feinberg responsible for potential deficits. (ANI)
