news.title: Todd Blanche as Trump’s new attorney general is a ‘red alert’ for abortion rights, groups warn
news.text:
Reproductive health advocates fear newly confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche will usher in a new wave of restrictions on abortion — even in states where it is legal.

Blanche’s confirmation “is a red alert for reproductive rights,” according to Nancy Northup, president and CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights. “The Attorney General’s job is to fairly and faithfully enforce the law, but Blanche appears willing to contort it to score wins for political allies,” she said Saturday.

Blanche has “openly vowed to use that power to ban abortion,” Gowri Buddiga, interim managing director for the group Free & Just, said in a statement shared with The Independent Saturday.

“From promising to restrict access to medication abortion through the mail, to gutting protections for patients and providers, Blanche will roll back access to care everywhere even in states where abortion is currently protected,” Buddiga said.

Blanche, who was confirmed in the early morning hours on Saturday by a narrow 50-49 vote, alarmed abortion advocates after leaked audio captured Trump’s former criminal defense attorney vowing to make the 2022 Supreme Court decision overturning the right to an abortion “permanent in every single state.” 

“We don’t have complete victory yet, but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and it will be permanent,” Blanche said, according to Politico, which obtained the now-deleted clip. 

“If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that,” he reportedly added. “They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.”

The Independent has contacted the Department of Justice for comment.

The Justice Department previously told The Independent that the comments “need to be understood in their full context, which was with respect to mail order abortion drugs, not a broader expansion of federal control over states.”

Much to the chagrin of anti-abortion campaigners, abortions have actually increased since the constitutional right to abortion care was struck down at the Supreme Court, thanks to a mix of expanded telehealth access, Biden-era policies and blue state “shield laws” protecting physicians who provide abortion care. 

While much of the attention in Blanche’s confirmation was directed at a now-abandoned $1.8 billion“slush fund” for the president’s political allies and a provision that shields the president from IRS investigations, Blanche’s appointment battle suggests the Trump administration could pursue more restrictions on abortion access.

Under questioning, he committed to reviewing the the Justice Department’s interpretation of the 1873 Comstock Act, which makes it illegal to send a variety of objects including “abortion-causing articles” via mail.

A 2022 Justice Department opinion held that the law doesn’t inherently bar sending abortion medication, given that “there are manifold ways in which recipients in every state may lawfully use such drugs, including to produce an abortion.”

On the campaign trail, Donald Trump described regulation around mail-order abortion drugs as a state issue, rather than a federal one, adding that he wouldn’t use the 19th century law to crack down on abortion access. 

 “The federal government should have nothing to do with this issue,” he said in 2024.

Republicans in the Senate have also pushed the federal government to settle lawsuits around mifepristone, a widely used abortion drug.

During his confirmation hearing, Blanche pointed to the FDA’s ongoing review of mifepristone. In 2023, the Biden administration ended in-person dispensing requirements around the drug, prompting challenges in Republican states.

“We have to have studies that we can defend in court,” he told senators in July. 

In May, the Supreme Court continued to block nationwide restrictions on mifepristone after a conservative appeals court cut off mail-order and telehealth access the drug, threatening access to millions of patients.

The president has vowed to be “the most pro-life and pro-family president in American history.”

In 2022, the Supreme Court, thanks to the conservative supermajority Trump helped appoint, overturned the landmark 1973 decision in Roe v Wade, which had established a constitutional right to an abortion.
news.summary: Blanche alarmed advocates by telling faith leaders ‘victory will be permanent’ in fight to restrict abortion access
news.author: Josh Marcus

Sophie Cunningham slams WNBA rival for 'playing the race card' after she claimed 'white privilege' caused her to be kicked off the court for brutal foul that left Fever star bloodied

MORE: Caitlin Clark faces WNBA suspension after another clash with officials

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

By DANIEL MATTHEWS, US SENIOR SPORTS WRITER

Published: 00:27 BST, 9 August 2026 | Updated: 00:48 BST, 9 August 2026

Sophie Cunningham has slammed DiJonai Carrington for 'playing' the race 'card' after the Chicago Sky star appeared to suggest her rival benefited from 'white privilege' during Saturday's shocking fracas. 

Carrington was ejected from the clash between the Sky and the Indiana Fever after her nasty foul left Cunningham bloodied and on the floor. 

Toward the end of the first quarter, Cunningham drove towards the basket, only to be struck in the face by Carrington's arm.

The Sky star was assessed a flagrant 2 and sent to the locker room, with both Cunningham and her teammate Caitlin Clark seen waving as Carrington headed to the locker room.

Minutes later, Carrington posted on social media: 'WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever.' But after the game, which ended in a 90-86 win for the Fever, Cunningham dismissed her rival's comment.

'I think the league is taking care of that. This has nothing to do with race,' she told ESPN. 'Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card.' 

A furious Sophie Cunningham had to be held back after she was floored by a nasty foul 

Cunningham drove towards the basket, only to be struck in the face by DiJonai Carrington

The Indiana Fever star was left bloodied by the incident, which provoked a furious reaction

Carrington, who was ejected, later wrote on social media: 'WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever'

Donald Trump Jr weighs in on WNBA trans carnage and ex-NBA star's attempts to get drafted

The Daily Mail has contacted the WNBA for comment. 

On the incident, Cunningham added: 'Clearly, I think it was like unnecessary. I've never really spoken to her and have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent up stuff. So get your s*** off. That's fine. I can take it.'

Cunningham suggested Carrington was simply 'craving' attention. 'I do think when people play the Fever, we're nationally televised, there's a lot of eyes on us and people just want attention. And that's her just trying to get attention,' she continued.

'I don't even know her. She wasn't even on the team last year when all that was going on... it's intentional. She wasn't even on the team. She has no reason to be doing any of that. So, good way to get her kicked out.'

Following the foul, Cunningham immediately climbed to her feet and attempted to confront Carrington, only for teammates and staff to drag her away. 

Footage from courtside appeared to show Cunningham calling her rival a 'dumb a** b****' and shouting: 'Why the f*** would you do that?' 

After the game, however, Cunningham insisted: 'I wasn't even upset... I popped up. I'm not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that's why she did it because she wants attention. 

'I mean, s***, people have started craving attention. Like, go get it somewhere else. Go do something good in the world.' 

Cunningham and Caitlin Clark were seen waving as Carrington headed to the locker room

Carrington was ejected after officials reviewed the foul and upgraded it to a flagrant 2

Cunningham has been at the center of a sporting and political firestorm in recent weeks after comments she made about transgender athletes. 

The Indiana Fever star said she wants to 'protect young girls' from 'biological men,' sparking demonstrations but also support from the likes of JD Vance.

It is not the first time that Carrington has been embroiled in a controversy involving one of the league's biggest stars, either.

Back in 2024, while playing for the Connecticut Sun, she left Clark with a black eye after poking the Fever guard in the face. 

No foul was called and Clark insisted the eye poke 'wasn't intentional,' while Carrington later appeared to mock the incident by staging a dramatic recreation in a social media stream.

news.title: Hunter Biden Calls Trump the ‘Singular Existential Threat’ to Planet Earth
news.text:
Hunter Biden doesn’t have plans of running for office himself, but he still has some strong opinions when it comes to the presidency. In fact, President Joe Biden’s son just called President Donald Trump “the singular existential threat” to planet Earth.

During his wide-ranging interview with BBC Newsnight’s Paddy O’Connell on Friday, the 56-year-old artist opened up about receiving a pardon from his father during his last weeks in office back in December 2024 — and how Trump’s behavior may have impacted the decision.

“I am the most privileged person, as it relates to that, that there could possibly be. I was one of one, and I am eternally grateful for it,” Hunter shared. “I am eternally grateful for it because I think that Donald Trump has proven to be exactly who my dad thought he was going to be, as it relates to the revenge and retribution that he would seek on his political enemies.”

“Was it good for our Constitution? Was it good for the American people? Was it good for my dad’s legacy? No, on all counts,” he further admitted.

President Biden pardoned his son just weeks ahead of his sentencing on tax evasion and federal gun charges. At the time, Trump called the act “an abuse and miscarriage of justice.” A year and half later, Hunter remains equally unimpressed by his father’s successor (who was also, notably, his predecessor).

“I’m not going to stop talking about Donald Trump,” he concluded. “Donald Trump is the singular existential threat to this globe. Donald Trump is, literally, a greater threat than we have faced in any of our lifetimes.”

Elsewhere in his interview, Hunter fought tears while sharing a painful update on his father’s prostate cancer metastasizing to his bones: “My dad is, to this day, remains the center of our family. Not just because of who he is as the the public person, but completely because of who he is to each one of us. It’s really, really hard and it’s really sad to watch.”
news.summary:
"Donald Trump is, literally, a greater threat than we have faced in any of our lifetimes," President Joe Biden's son adds

news.title: Team Trump Trolls Taylor Swift After 'August' Muted on Its TikTok
news.text:
Taylor Swift’s song “August” disappeared from a Team Trump TikTok video on Friday, days after the account used the track in a clip celebrating President Donald Trump and taunted the pop star in its caption.

The @TeamTrump account, which has 14 million followers and launched ahead of the 2024 election, posted the video earlier in the week using the song from Swift’s 2020 album “Folklore.” The clip showed Trump and first lady Melania Trump standing on a balcony watching fireworks, overlaid with text reading, “Mood because it’s August and Donald Trump is your president.”

The caption needled Swift directly.

“I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august,” the account wrote.

@teamtrump I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august ♬ som original – ⸆⸉ ོ

U.S. users noticed Friday evening that the audio had been stripped. A message on the video now reads that the copyright owner has not made the sound available. Neither Swift’s representatives nor the Trump campaign has said what caused the removal, and it remains unclear whether Swift or the rights holders for her music pulled the track.

Swift’s fans celebrated the disappearance in the comments.

“TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO QUEEEEEEN,” one user wrote.

Rather than drop the exchange, Team Trump leaned in. The account posted a follow-up TikTok using a live version of Swift’s 2012 track “Red,” pairing it with mocked-up album artwork featuring Trump’s face and a fake “Red (Trump’s Version)” playlist.

“Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican Party,” the post read.

The video rewrote several of Swift’s song titles to fit Republican messaging. “Everything Has Changed” became “Everything Has Changed (At Our Southern Border),” while “The Last Time” was reworked to “The Last Time (An Autopen Runs the Country).”

“August” was not the only song scrubbed from the account. Videos using Swift’s 2025 tracks “Father Figure” and “Opalite” also lost their audio, while a clip on the White House TikTok soundtracked with her song “The Fate of Ophelia” remained available.

Trump declared “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” on Truth Social in 2024 and later said the pop star was “no longer hot,” after Swift endorsed Kamala Harris for president ahead of the 2024 election. A month before that endorsement, Trump shared AI-generated images falsely suggesting Swift had backed his campaign, including one portraying her as Uncle Sam.
news.summary:
Taylor Swift's song "August" disappeared from a Team Trump TikTok video on Friday, days after the account used the track in a clip celebrating President Donald Trump and taunted the pop star in its caption.

news.title: Car bomb attack rattles Colombia after inauguration of hardline president  - Antigua Tribune – Daily
news.text:
Authorities have reported a car bomb attack in southwestern Colombia, one day after far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as president.

The country’s military alleged that the Saturday attack was carried out by two armed groups that splintered from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), a former rebel group that disarmed after a peace deal with the government in 2016.

Authorities say the attack targeted a toll plaza on the Pan-American Highway in the coastal department of Cauca, in the west of the country.

Two security guards reportedly suffered minor injuries in the explosion, which a witness said was carried out by an individual who left his car behind, then escaped the scene via motorcycle.

The administration of President de la Espriella quickly pledged a stern response to the car bombing.

“Colombia will not kneel before violence, nor will it allow the destruction of the infrastructure that connects our regions,” Minister of Transportation Elsa Noguera said in a social media post responding to the bombing.

She proceeded to reference de la Espriella’s inaugural speech, wherein he pledged to “defeat narco-terrorism” and tamp down criminal activity.

“As President Abelardo de la Espriella said yesterday, the time for restoring order has begun,” Noguera added. “We will recover security, control of our territories, and the peace of mind of Colombians.”

The hardline president, who was inaugurated on Friday, had campaigned for office on a promise to lead a crackdown on Colombia’s armed groups.

For more than six decades, Colombia has contended with an internal armed conflict between right-wing paramilitaries, left-wing rebels, government forces and criminal networks. The country is also the world’s largest producer of coca, the raw ingredient used to produce cocaine as well as traditional Andean medicines.

De la Espriella, a political newcomer, will join a handful of other right-wing figures across Latin America who successfully capitalised on concerns over crime and insecurity to win office.

But he is likely to face challenges addressing those deeply entrenched issues during the four years of his term. Colombian presidents are not eligible for re-election.

De la Espriella narrowly defeated his leftist opponent, Senator Ivan Cepeda, in a June run-off election that saw the two candidates separated by less than 1 percent of the vote.

The right-wing leader has said he would end the “Total Peace” approach of his predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, who became Colombia’s first-ever left-wing leader in 2022.

The “Total Peace” plan hinged on fostering dialogue with armed groups, though Petro did use military force as well.

By contrast, de la Espriella has pledged to return Colombia to a more militarised approach, saying in his inaugural speech that the option of dialogue was “exhausted”.

He has received support from United States President Donald Trump, whose administration has promised $1bn in security aid after a period of tense relations with Petro.

The Trump administration has sought to expand US military involvement across Latin America in the name of combatting crime and narcotics trafficking.

It has also encouraged right-wing leaders across the region to embrace more hardline tactics in their efforts to stem criminal activity.

De la Espriella, for example, has pledged to bomb boats and planes suspected of carrying illicit drugs, in line with a similar campaign undertaken by Trump in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.

Those tactics, however, have raised concern from rights groups who warn of the potential for rights abuses by government forces.

news.title: Brazen Iran makes EIGHT demands of the US as it dangles opening the Strait of Hormuz in front of Trump... while launching another attack on allied ship in crucial waterway
news.text:
Iranian leadership has a dramatic new list of eight demands that the United States must follow to reach Donald Trump's goal of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. 

The key waterway has been closed for much of the time since the war on Iran began in late February. 

Iran's politburo-like body known as the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) said the Strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States 'corrects its behavior,' issuing new demands that could shake up talks on a deal to manage the waterway and traffic on it. 

The head of Iran's SNSC, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, has given the list that includes some previously unheard of requests. 

Many have been previously brought up, including ending the war permanently, stopping the US Naval blockade, withdrawing military forces. 

From there, Zolghadr wants the US end sanctions on Tehran, unfreeze Iranian assets and even pay reparations to the Iranians to reopen the strait. 

The US would also have to stop threatening and insulting Iran and end all military action against Iranian allies in the region, state news agency Islamic Republic News Agency reports. 

Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the powerful Revolutionary Guard, reports directly to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who is currently mulling over a deal with Oman to manage the strait. 

A 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended. 

The Daily Mail has reached out to the State Department for comment.

Iran's demands come on the same day the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile in the strait.

The requests also arrive as Donald Trump has attempted to quash reports that he and Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth have clashed over reports the United States has hidden missile shortages.

Confronted over why the President was kept in the dark, the secretary of war reportedly turned on his own deputy, according to the Washington Post. 

The showdown reportedly unfolded at Camp David last Friday, where Hegseth insisted he was blameless and accused his number two, Stephen Feinberg, of presiding over the shortfall and failing to keep the President fully briefed. 

The astonishing scene laid bare Trump's mounting frustration with Hegseth, one of the loudest early cheerleaders for striking Iran, who had assured him the operation would be a swift and relatively painless win. 

Shortages of long-range guided missiles and air defense interceptors are among the reasons Trump has held back from launching further large-scale strikes against Iran in recent days. 

Trump hit back at the report, denying any shortage of US munitions and insisting that interceptors are reaching American bases as needed.

'The “leakers” of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!' Trump wrote on Truth Social. 

The White House has denied the clash ever took place, however, with press secretary Karoline Leavitt saying: 'This is 100% fake news. Literally never happened. And President Trump has the utmost confidence in Secretary Hegseth.'

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell joined the pushback, insisting Hegseth 'did not mislead anyone' about weapons stocks and never pointed the finger at Feinberg

Despite the denials, NBC News reported that Feinberg received a furious phone call from Trump himself on Friday evening, during which the President is said to have threatened to fire him.

The rattled deputy then hastily summoned top Pentagon brass to a late-night crisis meeting just hours after hanging up.

Feinberg, 66, is a billionaire who chaired Trump's Intelligence Advisory Board in his first term before being handed the Pentagon's number two job.

The interceptor crunch is reportedly now so severe that it is changing how the military decides which incoming threats to shoot down. 

Commanders are forced to weigh where a missile is headed before committing precious defenses. 

Far from the quick victory Trump was promised, the Iran conflict has ground into a near six-month stalemate, with 18 American troops dead. 

Tehran has responded to these attacks by raining missiles on American bases and allies across the region and strangling shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz.

A fragile truce brokered by Pakistan collapsed last month after Iranian attacks on tankers.

Trump declared US forces 'locked and loaded' for fresh strikes at the weekend, only to back down after appeals from Gulf allies, and he now claims talks with Tehran are restarting, something Iran denies.
news.summary: The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, has given the list that includes some previously unheard of requests.

news.title: Russia Sanctions Bill: 3 Roadblocks Could Delay US Tariffs On India, China
news.text: The US Senate’s Russia sanctions bill, which could pave the way for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on India, China and three other countries over purchases of Russian energy, faces three major hurdles before it can reach President Donald Trump for approval. The legislation must first clear the House of Representatives, which is currently on summer recess until August 31. A potential vote in September could also clash with an expected meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. At the same time, opposition is growing among House Democrats and at least one senior Republican to provisions that would give the administration sweeping tariff powers. House schedule creates first hurdle The House’s legislative calendar leaves lawmakers with a limited window to consider the bill. Members return on August 31 but are expected to spend much of October and early November campaigning ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. That means a House vote could take place as early as September, although political and diplomatic considerations could push consideration to later in the year. Trump-Xi summit could complicate timing September could prove particularly sensitive because of the expected Trump-Xi summit, currently anticipated for September 24. The White House may be reluctant to push legislation threatening tariffs on China through the House immediately before the meeting, as Washington seeks to maintain a stable atmosphere in US-China relations. The bill would also affect China, one of the world’s largest buyers of Russian energy. Opposition to tariff powers grows The legislation has faced opposition from senior House Democrats who argue that its tariff provisions give the president excessive authority. House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking Democrat Gregory Meeks and Democratic Representative Don Beyer have called the current version of the bill “unacceptable”, arguing that it could allow Trump to impose additional tariffs while reducing congressional oversight. An amendment introduced by Republican Senator Rand Paul and Democratic Senator Ron Wyden to remove the tariff provisions failed in the Senate. However, 32 senators supported the amendment, indicating significant bipartisan opposition to the tariff powers. If the House changes the legislation, the Senate would have to approve the revised version before it could reach Trump. Why India faces a fresh tariff risk The bill could have significant implications for India as New Delhi and Washington continue negotiations on an interim trade agreement. The legislation names India, China, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan as countries subject to potential tariff action over purchases of Russian energy. The US Trade Representative would determine the actual tariff rate, with a maximum ceiling of 100 per cent. The president would also have the authority to waive the tariffs on national-interest grounds, although such waivers would be subject to periodic review. For India, the legislation could create an additional source of tariff pressure beyond the measures already under discussion between New Delhi and Washington. India-US trade talks in focus The potential legislation comes as India and the US work towards finalising an interim trade arrangement. A February 7 framework had envisaged reducing the effective tariff on Indian exports significantly, including a penalty previously linked to India’s purchases of Russian oil. However, the proposed Russia sanctions legislation would create a separate tariff mechanism targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy. This means the outcome of the House debate could become an important factor in India-US trade negotiations, particularly if lawmakers retain the bill’s tariff provisions. For now, the legislation faces a difficult path through the House, with its timing, opposition to tariff powers and the potential impact on US-China relations emerging as three major obstacles before it can reach Trump’s desk.
news.summary: The US Senate's sanctions bill targeting Russia may impose tariffs up to 100% on India, China, and others for Russian energy purchases, but it faces significant challenges.

news.title: Kerala jaunt for Trump son-in-law Michael Boulos during private visit with US envoy
news.text:
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Michael Boulos arrived in Kerala on a whirlwind private trip on Saturday, accompanied by US ambassador to India Sergio Gor.

Boulos, Tiffany Trump’s husband, landed with his seven-member team in Bengaluru on Friday and reached Kochi on Saturday. From there, they proceeded to Alappuzha, where they witnessed the trial run of two 100-foot snake boats in the famous Punnamada Lake ahead of the 72nd Nehru Trophy Boat Race on August 22. The delegation left Kerala on Saturday evening.

The Kerala police said they got information about the trip on Friday. The police have not revealed the itinerary of the US delegation, but a source told The Telegraph that the delegation stayed at Hyatt in Kochi and travelled via road to Alappuzha.

“Boulos, Gor and the rest of the delegation reached Alappuzha by 2pm. They enjoyed the beauty of the backwaters in Alappuzha and a houseboat ride in Punnamada Lake. Gor told the media in Alappuzha that he would have loved to stay back in Kerala for a few more days, but time constraints were forcing him to return to New Delhi.

“I called on Kerala chief minister V.D. Satheesan in Kochi on Saturday and talked on various sectors. This is my first visit to the state. I’m hugely impressed by its natural beauty, rich cultural heritage and its considerable potential as an international tourism destination,” Gor said.

In a statement, Satheesan said he highlighted the scope for closer partnerships between universities and research institutions in Kerala and the US, including joint research, academic exchanges and innovation partnerships.

“The ambassador expressed his interest in facilitating greater engagement between American companies and Kerala and in connecting more US businesses with investment opportunities in the state. The meeting also considered ways to deepen engagement with the Kerala community and business networks in the US,” he added.

The chief minister has proposed an invest desk in the US to facilitate investment enquiries, connect prospective investors and companies with opportunities in Kerala, and strengthen engagement with the Kerala diaspora and the wider US business community.

news.title: Oil Prices fall over 9% as USA-Iran tensions ease
news.text:
By Boluwatife Oshadiya | August 9, 2026

Brent crude fell 9.21% for the week to $81.81 per barrel as optimism over US-Iran diplomacy reduced geopolitical risk

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) declined 9.4% to $76.71 per barrel, while expectations of higher OPEC+ supply added pressure

A 2.5 million-barrel increase in US crude inventories reinforced expectations of a better-supplied market

Oil prices fell more than 9% during the week as improving prospects for US-Iran diplomacy eased fears of supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.

International benchmark Brent crude ended at $81.81 per barrel, down 9.21% from $90.11 a week earlier, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) declined 9.4% to $76.71 from $84.67.

The decline followed renewed optimism over diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran after US President Donald Trump said talks with Iran had resumed and were making progress.

The prospect of an agreement reducing risks around the Strait of Hormuz encouraged investors to unwind part of the geopolitical premium that had supported crude prices.

Supply expectations also weighed on the market. Major OPEC+ producers agreed to increase collective production by 188,000 barrels per day from September as the group continues to reverse voluntary production cuts introduced in 2023.

US inventory data added further pressure. Commercial crude inventories unexpectedly increased by about 2.5 million barrels during the week, contrary to forecasts for a decline.

Oil prices recovered some ground toward the end of the week as uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz continued to provide a degree of support.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi also indicated that discussions with Oman over future shipping arrangements in the strait were nearing completion, while reports of possible restrictions on vessels from countries Tehran considers hostile kept supply concerns in focus.

What’s Being Said

US President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran had resumed and were making progress, a position that helped reduce the geopolitical risk premium in oil markets.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi has separately said Tehran was working with Oman on arrangements for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Current reporting, however, indicates that the status of direct US-Iran negotiations remains contested, with Iranian officials disputing some US claims about the talks.

What’s Next

Oil traders will watch developments around the Strait of Hormuz, particularly any agreement that could restore more normal shipping activity through the strategic waterway.

Markets will also monitor OPEC+ production increases and subsequent US inventory data for evidence of whether global supply conditions are loosening further.

The Bottom Line:

The sharp weekly decline shows that oil prices are responding to a combination of lower geopolitical risk and stronger supply expectations. However, continued uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz means the market remains sensitive to any reversal in diplomatic or shipping developments.

news.title: US Senate advances landmark crypto bill before heading on August recess
news.text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 8 (Reuters) - U.S. Senate Majority ⁠Leader John Thune moved on Saturday to advance a major bill that would create ⁠a regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies which, if passed, would mark a huge victory ‌for U.S. President Donald Trump and the crypto industry.

Thune, a Republican, early Saturday morning filed to set up a key procedural vote on the Clarity Act when the Senate returns from its August recess in mid-September, potentially paving the ​way for a full floor vote on the bill, according ⁠to the U.S. Senate Press Gallery ⁠website.

The move suggests Senate Republican leaders believe they may yet be able to wrangle the 60 ⁠votes ‌needed for the bill to pass, despite continued opposition by many Democrats. Currently, the bill needs the support of at least eight Democrats and all of the Senate's voting ⁠Republicans for it to pass.

The legislation would give the crypto ​industry its first comprehensive federal ‌rulebook, defining when digital tokens are securities or commodities and which regulators oversee them. ⁠Crypto companies say ​the act is necessary to provide legal clarity for the industry and could potentially boost the adoption of cryptocurrencies.

The passage of the Clarity Act would also hand Trump a second major crypto policy win after ⁠he signed a bill supporting dollar-backed tokens known as stablecoins ​into law last year, even as Democrats say his family's own crypto profits create a conflict of interest.

The crypto industry spent more than $119 million backing pro-crypto candidates in the 2024 election hoping to ⁠advance the Clarity Act and stablecoin law.

Passage of the bill would be a blow for banks, which have fought to limit language that would allow crypto companies to effectively compete for bank deposits by offering rewards on customer stablecoin holdings.

Trump, who courted crypto cash on the campaign trail ​and whose family has profited from its own token, has prioritized ⁠crypto reform during his second administration and the White House has also been pushing hard for the ​bill, Reuters reported.

Trump in June reported more than $1.4 billion in ‌income from his family's crypto ventures last year.

Democrats ​want more restrictions on government officials' crypto ventures, and negotiations on that aspect of the bill remain fluid.

 (Reporting by Hannah Lang and Michelle Price; Editing by Nia Williams)

news.title: Patriot Games vs Presidential Fitness Test: biggest differences explained
news.text:
With Donald Trump's Patriot Games set to take place in celebration of America's 250th anniversary, here's a breakdown of how the new event compares to the Presidential Fitness Test. 

Alongside being compared to a real-life The Hunger Games, the Trump's Patriot Games have also been compared to the school physical evaluation program initiated in 1956 by President Dwight D. Eisenhower.

The newly-introduced games take place from August 9-11, but as America prepares for the inaugural event, there are still a lot of questions to answer - especially when comparing it to the pre-existing Presidential Fitness Test, which students across the US already take to 'build strength, endurance, and healthy habits', according to the White House website.

Why were the two programs created in the first place? What exactly do the two programs consist of, who takes part and what do you get out of taking part?

What is the Presidential Fitness Test?

Established long before the Patriot Games, back in 1956, the Presidential Fitness Test was created by President Dwight D. Eisenhower in a bid to strengthen young people in America to match the health and fitness of those in Europe.

It was phased out in 2013 and replaced by the Presidential Youth Fitness Program.

However, in July 2025 it was reinstated against with updated guidelines from the White House.

What are the Patriot Games?

Created by Trump, the Patriot Games are being organized by Freedom 250 - the group put together to coordinate the celebrations of the 250th Anniversary of American Independence - and they're intended to celebrate 'the next generation'.

The games will bring young people together to 'compete, inspire, and showcase the values that have shaped the United States for nearly 250 years,' as per Freedom 250's website.

The Patriot Games will celebrate the America's 250th anniversary (Freedom 250) 

Who can take part in each of the events?

The Presidential Fitness Test 

The Presidential Fitness Test can be taken by anyone aged six to 17 and over, as per the White House's website.

The Patriot Games

In comparison, the Patriot Games are much more exclusive.

High school athletes aged between 14 and 17 are eligible to take part and 'represent America's great states and territories, alongside athletes from tribal nations', though they must be 14 years old by June 1, 2026 or be 17 or younger as of December 31, 2026.

Parents and guardians must also approve the student's application.

Physical challenges 

The Presidential Fitness Test 

The test is meant to provide students with 'clear, age-appropriate benchmarks that encourage them to build strength, endurance, and healthy habits while striving for personal improvement'.

Physical challenges include core strength exercises such as curl-ups or planking, and cardio challenges such as a one mile run or 20m beep test.

It also challenges you to an upper body exercise such as right-angle push-ups or pull-ups, setting certain benchmarks across all three categories.

The Patriot Games

While the Patriot Games will test individual strength, it will also put teamwork to the test.

"The event will feature a series of athletic challenges designed to test strength, endurance, agility, teamwork, and perseverance while highlighting the values that have helped shape generations of Americans," Freedom 250 explains.

Military.com reports this is set to see traditional American sports combined with more boot camp style and obstacle course challenges.

Competition vs assessment 

The Presidential Fitness Test 

Rather than students competing against one another, the Presidential Fitness Test sets certain benchmarks for participants to measure themselves against national standards.

The Patriot Games

The Patriot Games, however, does indeed set students against one another, offering one male and one female champion the chance to claim first place.

But what do they get for taking part or, in the case of the games, winning?

The Presidential Fitness Test 

If you complete the Presidential Fitness Test you can receive a Certificate of Participation

Should you meet the established fitness benchmarks, you're in with the chance of making two award levels - Presidential and National.

"Together, these recognition levels encourage students to set goals, track progress, and celebrate their accomplishments," the White House adds.

While the Patriot Games is far more competitive.

The Patriot Games

The games is a competition, offering a staggering $125,000 scholarship prize one male and one female champion - a total prize pool of $250,000.

"Creating life-changing opportunities for young Americans while inspiring millions across the country," Freedom250 states.

President Trump first announced the games in a video in December.

The Patriot Games are set to take place between August 9 and 11 at Spire Academy in Geneva, Ohio, and competition coverage will be streamed on the ESPN app.

news.title: Mark Zuckerberg hammered after ignoring distress call for stranded vessel: report
news.text:
Billionaire and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg was hit with “unanimous booing” this week for reportedly ignoring a request from the U.S. Coast Guard to rescue a stranded sea vessel from his $300 million yacht, the Alaska Beacon reported Saturday.

“I’m on a small-ship Alaska cruise with my son,” reads a social media post from Michael Love, a New York software developer. “Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this).”

According to vessel tracking services reviewed by the Alaska Beacon, Love’s account appeared accurate, confirming that Zuckerberg’s yacht was “slowing to a halt outside Farragut Bay,” a five-mile wide bay in southern Alaska, south of its capital city, Juneau.

Love claimed the stranded vessel – known as the Uncruise Wilderness Legacy – had two women, a child and a dog onboard and was “going too far with too little gas.”

“We gave them some [gas] and helped find an anchorage for the night,” Love wrote in a follow-up social media post.

When asked by the Alaska Beacon, Love said it was puzzling as to why the crew of Zuckerberg’s yacht ignored the Coast Guard’s radio call.

“Frankly, if I was Mark Zuckerberg I would be absolutely ecstatic at a chance to do something helpful for someone in need and maybe get some good PR out of it,” Love said.

Zuckerberg has faced scrutiny for his apparent alignment with President Donald Trump and his administration in recent years.

Zuckerberg dined with Trump at Mar-a-Lago shortly after the 2024 election, praised Trump's reaction to his first assassination attempt as "bad---," and restored Trump's Facebook account following its post-Jan. 6 suspension. He later sat beside Trump at a September 2025 White House dinner for tech executives, where Meta pledged at least $600 billion in U.S. infrastructure investment through 2028, and in March 2026, Trump named Zuckerberg to his newly formed Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
